$comment: The OpenHands hooks wiring for lypning, as a standalone fragment.

`lypning install --harness openhands` does NOT write this file, and will not write it for you. It installs a plugin directory instead — ~/.openhands/plugins/lypning/ — which OpenHands discovers ambiently and merges into every conversation, so no file the user owns is edited at all. This copy is for the other case: someone who would rather wire the hooks themselves.

MERGE, DO NOT REPLACE — and understand that this file is the one place where that is not enough. HookConfig.load() is FIRST-MATCH-WINS AND NOT MERGED: it reads <working_dir>/.openhands/hooks.json, and only if that is absent, ~/.openhands/hooks.json. So a second hooks.json does not add to the first, it HIDES it. If you already have one of these files, add the three entries below to it by hand; do not drop this file over the top of it, and do not create a project-level one while relying on a user-level one.

That asymmetry is exactly why the installer declines this route. There is no per-entry ownership marker in this format, so lypning could not later remove only its own entries the way it can in .claude/settings.json — and an uninstall that cannot be exact is an uninstall that costs the user something they had.
SessionEnd is deliberately NOT async. The SDK's AsyncProcessManager terminates outstanding async hook processes at session end, so an async harvest is one that gets killed partway through writing.

PostToolUse IS async: fire-and-forget, stdout and stderr to DEVNULL, off the agent's critical path entirely. It is structurally incapable of blocking the tool call, which is the strongest form of the rule that a capture harness never blocks.

PostToolUse rather than PreToolUse, and never both: two hooks on one tool would write two records per call, and since the harvester counts distinct occurrence keys, that would silently double the count that `lypning conformance --plan` steers by. The cost of choosing PostToolUse is real — commands typed and then denied never reach it, and those are evidence of what the model types. What it buys is the observation: exit code and output, from a CPython run you paid for anyway.

The matcher is exactly "terminal" — the registry key, derived by ToolDefinition.__init_subclass__ from the class name. "TerminalTool" appears in the SDK's own docstring examples and is stale; a matcher spelled that way matches nothing, forever, and says nothing about it.

The commands are PATH-resolved console-script names on purpose. There is no plugin-root variable expansion in the SDK, and the hook executor sets cwd to the WORKSPACE — so a relative path would resolve against your repository, not against wherever this file lives.

Every one of these exits 0 on every path, including its own failures, and emits no "decision" key. OpenHands treats exit code 2 as BLOCK and honours a "decision" of "allow" or "deny" in stdout JSON; lypning sends neither, for the same reason its Claude Code hook sends no permissionDecision — bypassing a permission prompt is far more than a capture harness may do.
Off switches, no edit required: LYPNING_CAPTURE=0 disables the whole harness, LYPNING_HARVEST=0 keeps capturing but stops the SessionEnd hook publishing.
